title: H-1B for Entrepreneurs: What Indian Workers Need to Know About Transferring a Visa to Their Own Startup
excerpt: A growing number of H-1B holders are exploring the path from employee to founder, but the legal hurdles remain significant and the process demands careful planning.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • H-1B holders can transfer their visa to their own startup with specific requirements.
  • Key requirements include a real office, prevailing wage, and a Board of Directors.
  • The International Entrepreneur Parole allows founders to work at startups with $250,000 investment.
  • Founders must avoid operational work while on H-1B to maintain visa status.
  • H-1B holders can legally transfer their visa to a company they own, but the startup must file a separate H-1B petition and meet all standard requirements as a sponsoring employer
  • Key requirements include a real office, ability to pay the prevailing wage, a specialty occupation role, and — critically — an employer-employee relationship enforced through a Board of Directors
  • The International Entrepreneur Parole (IEP) programme offers an alternative path, allowing founders with at least $250,000 in qualified U.S. investment to work at their startup for up to five years
  • Immigration attorneys warn that founders must avoid any operational work for their startup while still employed under their current H-1B or risk violating their visa status

For thousands of Indian tech workers in the United States, the dream is familiar: build something of your own. But for those on H-1B visas — a category in which Indians account for roughly 72% of all approvals — the path from corporate employee to startup founder is fraught with legal complexity that can jeopardise their immigration status if mishandled.

A recent analysis by immigration law firm Lexology has reignited discussion about a question that H-1B holders have long grappled with: can you transfer your H-1B to your own startup? The short answer is yes, but with significant caveats that every aspiring immigrant founder should understand.

How the Transfer Works

Under current USCIS rules, an H-1B holder's own company can file an H-1B change-of-employer petition on their behalf. The catch is that the company must meet every requirement that any other H-1B sponsor would face: a legitimate business with a real office, the financial capacity to pay the prevailing wage, and a role that qualifies as a specialty occupation.

The most critical — and counterintuitive — requirement is the employer-employee relationship. When the visa holder is also the company's owner, USCIS needs assurance that someone can hire, fire, and supervise them. For founders who hold a majority stake, this means establishing a Board of Directors with the authority to control the visa holder's employment.

"USCIS looks at whether the company, as an entity separate from the individual, has the right to control the beneficiary's work. Owners with more than 50% equity face the highest scrutiny."

— Fragomen, Del Rey, Bernsen & Loewy LLP

    What You Can and Cannot Do While Planning

    The line between permissible planning and unauthorised work is razor-thin. While still employed under their current H-1B, aspiring founders may brainstorm business models, hire attorneys and consultants, and conduct high-level planning. They may not sign vendor agreements, manage employees, open the business for operations, or sell or market their product.

    USCIS has previously denied H-1B petitions where founders were found to have performed "productive work" for their startup before the transfer was approved. Even unpaid advisory work has been treated as a violation in some cases.

    Once the new H-1B petition is filed, however, the visa holder can begin working for their startup immediately — they do not need to wait for approval. Some attorneys recommend waiting for the approval to arrive before making the switch, as protection against a potential denial.

    The IEP Alternative

    For founders who cannot meet the traditional H-1B transfer requirements, the International Entrepreneur Parole (IEP) programme offers another route. Revived after years of regulatory limbo, IEP allows foreign-born entrepreneurs to work at their U.S. startup for up to five years if they can demonstrate:

    • At least 10% ownership in a U.S. startup formed within the past five years
    • A central and active role in the company's operations
    • At least $250,000 in qualified funding from established U.S. investors, or $100,000 in government grants

    The programme supports up to three entrepreneurs per startup and does not count against the annual H-1B cap — a significant advantage given the lottery system that leaves tens of thousands of qualified applicants without visas each year.

    The Modernisation Rules

    Recent H-1B modernisation rules have further expanded the pathway for entrepreneurs. The updated regulations allow founders to sponsor themselves for H-1B visas under their own companies, provided they meet specific criteria. Initial approvals are limited to 18 months, and the founder must perform specialty occupation duties for a majority of their working time.

    The rule also introduces a "logical connection" standard between degree requirements and job duties, potentially reducing Requests for Evidence and simplifying the application process for startup roles that may not fit neatly into traditional job categories.

    Practical Advice for Indian Founders

    Immigration attorneys consistently recommend a methodical approach: continue working for your current employer while incorporating your startup and building its infrastructure. File a concurrent H-1B petition if you want to work part-time for both companies, or a change-of-employer petition when you are ready to transition fully.

    The stakes are high. A denied petition can trigger a loss of status, and the current political climate around H-1B visas adds uncertainty. But for those who navigate the process correctly, the reward is building a company in the world's largest economy while maintaining legal immigration status — a combination that has produced some of Silicon Valley's most successful Indian-American founders.
